claims.text: A highly uniform atomic distribution, extensive lattice strain, and a high density of grain boundaries enhance catalytic performance in noble-metal-based HEA nanomaterials.
Rapid quenching produces a uniform nanocrystalline structure in noble-metal-based HEA nanocatalysts.
The proposed initial material is a single-phase HEA.
The proposed initial material has grain sizes below 100 nm.
The proposed initial material has minimal phase segregation and significant lattice distortion.
Controlled thermal annealing promotes grain growth.
Reaction temperatures below 500 K preserve the nanostructure and alloy homogeneity.
The active structural state combines pronounced lattice distortion with a high density of grain boundaries.
Uniform atomic distribution, lattice strain, and grain boundaries alter the electronic structure of noble metals, including shifting the d-band center.
The electronic-structure changes fine-tune reactant adsorption energies.
Annealing-induced grain growth reduces lattice-strain effects.
Annealing-induced grain growth decreases the density of active grain boundaries.
Reduced strain and grain-boundary density lower catalytic activity.
As-deposited, rapidly quenched samples will have higher catalytic conversion rates than annealed samples with coarser grains.
As-deposited, rapidly quenched samples will have lower catalytic activation energy than annealed samples.
Conventional noble-metal catalysts or post-annealed HEA catalysts typically have greater phase heterogeneity and larger, less-strained grains.
The proposed mechanism applies principally to nanomaterials with grain sizes below approximately 100 nm.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to bulk materials or markedly different reaction environments.
Studies of refractory HEAs indicate that grain-boundary density and lattice distortion influence defect behavior.
Failure of annealing-induced grain growth and boundary-density reduction to measurably reduce catalytic performance would falsify the proposed structure–activity relationship.
